hotels.name: Astor Hyde Park
hotels.whyGo: A Victorian townhouse opposite the Royal Albert Hall with cornicing and fireplaces intact - a far better building than a hostel at this price should occupy.
hotels.opNote: Townhouse stairs and no lift, so not accessible and hard work with a big bag. Walking distance to the three free museums.

hotels.name: Clink78
hotels.whyGo: A former magistrates' court where some rooms are the original cells and the bar is in the old courtrooms - the Clash were tried in this building in 1978.
hotels.opNote: Ten minutes from King's Cross and St Pancras on foot. Private rooms exist and are worth it if dorms are not your thing.

hotels.name: Generator London
hotels.style: Party hostel in a former police building
hotels.whyGo: Seven hundred and fifty rooms, a bar built into a bus, and a 24-hour reception - the default answer if the point of the trip is meeting people.
hotels.opNote: IT IS A PARTY HOSTEL and does not pretend otherwise. Wrong choice for an early start or light sleepers; female-only dorms are available.

hotels.name: Nell Gwynn House Pod Rooms
hotels.style: Pod rooms in a 1930s mansion block
hotels.whyGo: Pod-format rooms inside a 1930s Chelsea mansion block, under a kilometre from the V&A and walkable to the three free South Kensington museums.
hotels.opNote: OPENED JANUARY 2026, so there is very little independent review history yet - treat the format claims as the operator's until that changes.

hotels.name: Otherwander Soho
hotels.typicalFrom: About £70 a single pod, £80 a double
hotels.whyGo: A brand-new capsule hotel on Dean Street with its own air conditioning, lighting and sockets in each pod, a few steps from the Dean Street entrance to the Elizabeth line.
hotels.opNote: YOU CANNOT STAND UP INSIDE A POD, and bathrooms are communal - clean and room-like, but shared. Reviewers report hearing corridor conversation and pod doors despite the soundproofing claim, and taller guests find the upper pods awkward.

hotels.name: The GreenHouse Capsules
hotels.whyGo: Capsule accommodation within a couple of kilometres of Brick Lane, at hostel-dorm prices but with the privacy of an enclosed pod.
hotels.opNote: OPENED JANUARY 2026 with no independent review history. The capsule format trades a window and a wardrobe for the price - the same bargain Zedwell makes, without the scale or the press.

hotels.name: Wombat's City Hostel London
hotels.style: Former sailors' hostel by Tower Bridge
hotels.whyGo: A refurbished sailors' hostel minutes from Tower Bridge and the Tower of London, with a proper kitchen, a free-food shelf and one of the better hostel bars.
hotels.opNote: A free drink voucher on check-in. The wooden bunks are reported as squeaky, which matters in a sixteen-bed room.

hotels.name: YHA London St Pancras
hotels.whyGo: Three minutes from St Pancras International, run by a charity, with a proper kitchen and none of the party-hostel apparatus.
hotels.opNote: The best hostel choice for an early Eurostar or anyone who wants to sleep. Wheelchair-accessible rooms, which is rare in this tier.

hotels.name: Zedwell Greenwich
hotels.whyGo: The same soundproofed windowless format as the Piccadilly flagship, at Greenwich prices and within reach of the Cutty Sark and the Observatory.
hotels.opNote: Windowless by design, as with every Zedwell. Cheaper than the Piccadilly site and far quieter at night.

hotels.name: Zedwell Piccadilly Circus
hotels.whyGo: Almost a thousand windowless, soundproofed 'cocoons' inside the Grade II London Pavilion on Piccadilly Circus - the largest capsule hotel in the world, from about £30 a night in zone 1.
hotels.opNote: EVERY ROOM IS WINDOWLESS BY DESIGN, not by accident - filtered air, blackout, no clutter, no wardrobe. Reviewers split hard: some call it the best sleep they have had in London, others find waking in pitch dark disorienting. Know which you are before booking.

hotels.name: Zedwell Tottenham Court Road
hotels.whyGo: Carved out of a disused underground car park beneath Great Russell Street - 206 soundproofed cocoons and London's first hotel that is entirely below ground.
hotels.opNote: Windowless is the whole concept here rather than a compromise, since the building has no surface at all. Two minutes from the British Museum and a short walk to the Tottenham Court Road Elizabeth line entrance.

hotels.name: citizenM London Bankside
hotels.whyGo: One room type, a wall-to-wall window, a tablet that runs the blinds and lights, and a lobby full of Eames and Panton that works as a living room.
hotels.opNote: Rooms are genuinely SMALL - the bed fills the width. That is the trade for the price and the location; people who have not seen the format are sometimes shocked.

hotels.name: hub by Premier Inn London Covent Garden
hotels.whyGo: Premier Inn's compact format - the bed fills the room, the lighting and heating run off an app - at a St Martin's Lane address that would otherwise cost triple.
hotels.opNote: ROOMS ARE ABOUT 11 SQUARE METRES and reviewers are regularly surprised by that. Same bed and same Which?-rated reliability as a standard Premier Inn, in a fraction of the space.

hotels.name: La Gaffe
hotels.whyGo: A small family-run hotel and Italian restaurant on the site of an 18th-century shepherd's cottage, five minutes' walk from the Heath.
hotels.opNote: Small and genuinely family-run rather than corporate, which is rare in this price band this close to the Heath. No lift; check room location if stairs are a problem.

hotels.name: nhow London
hotels.whyGo: Project Orange's punk-meets-high-tech interior, complete with a Big Ben rocket sculpture in the lobby and graffiti throughout - British iconography played entirely for fun.
hotels.opNote: Design-forward at a mid-range price, which is unusual. The theme is committed rather than tasteful; that is the point.

hotels.name: NOX Hotels Belsize Park
hotels.whyGo: A converted pub in Belsize Park, walkable to both the Heath and Primrose Hill and handy for the Belsize Park Northern line stop.
hotels.opNote: Rooms retain some of the building's pub-era character rather than a stripped, corporate refit - worth knowing if that appeals or does not.

hotels.name: Point A Hotel London King's Cross
hotels.style: Budget design rooms by the terminals
hotels.whyGo: Small, clean, quiet rooms with mood lighting, minutes from St Pancras - the sensible answer for a Eurostar arrival or an early departure.
hotels.opNote: Rooms are compact and most have no view worth the name. For a night either side of a train that is not a real cost.

hotels.name: Premier Inn London County Hall
hotels.style: Budget chain in a landmark building
hotels.familyPolicy: Two under-16s free in a family room
hotels.whyGo: Inside County Hall next to the London Eye, which is an absurd address for a budget chain - the same building as a five-star hotel, at a third of the price.
hotels.opNote: The best-located Premier Inn in London and priced accordingly - it is the most expensive in the estate. Book far ahead; walk-up rates are poor value.

hotels.name: Premier Inn London Stratford
hotels.style: Closest hotel to the Olympic Park
hotels.familyPolicy: Two under-16s free in a family room
hotels.whyGo: Under two hundred metres from Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park - the closest hotel to it of any kind, inside the Westfield complex.
hotels.opNote: KEPT ON MERIT after the 2026-08-20 chains review, on the same basis as County Hall - the proximity to the Olympic Park is a genuine standout, not just cheap-and-present.

hotels.name: Staycity Aparthotels Dalston
hotels.whyGo: Kitchens and washing machines on Kingsland High Street, in the middle of Dalston's bar and music strip rather than a business district.
hotels.opNote: FORMERLY KINGSLAND LOCKE - Staycity took the lease over in 2025, so older reviews and articles use the Locke name for the same building.

hotels.name: Strand Palace
hotels.style: Big art deco hotel on the Strand
hotels.whyGo: Nearly eight hundred rooms on the Strand, opened 1909, with an art deco frontage - the reliable large-scale option between Covent Garden and the river.
hotels.opNote: Its scale is the point: there is usually availability when the boutiques are full. The original 1930s deco entrance is in the V&A collection.

hotels.name: The Georgian House Hotel
hotels.whyGo: A nineteenth-century family-run townhouse whose lower ground floor holds the Wizard Chambers - four-poster beds, candles and potion bottles, the closest thing London has to a Harry Potter hotel.
hotels.opNote: The Wizard Chambers are SPECIFIC ROOMS, not the whole hotel - book them by name or you will get an ordinary (perfectly nice) townhouse room. Minutes from Victoria station.

hotels.name: The Grafton Arms
hotels.style: Boutique rooms over a Fitzrovia pub
hotels.whyGo: Eleven boutique rooms over a Fitzrovia pub with a roof terrace and a pan-Asian kitchen - a proper London pub downstairs and somewhere decent to sleep upstairs.
hotels.opNote: A pub building, so no lift and some noise from below at weekends. Minutes from Charlotte Street and Warren Street.

hotels.name: The Pilgrm
hotels.style: Independent, under a minute from the station
hotels.whyGo: Genuinely independent rather than a chain wearing a boutique name, in a converted Victorian building closer to the station than any of the branded alternatives.
hotels.opNote: The single best-placed hotel for a Heathrow Express arrival or an early departure - it is not an exaggeration to say under a minute's walk.

hotels.name: The Z Hotel Covent Garden
hotels.whyGo: A compact-room format that buys a Covent Garden postcode for mid-range money, with free cheese and wine in the lounge each evening.
hotels.opNote: THE CHEAPEST ROOMS HAVE NO WINDOW. They are sold as 'Inside' rooms and people book them by accident constantly. Pay up a grade unless you genuinely do not care.

hotels.name: The Z Hotel Shoreditch
hotels.style: Compact rooms, free evening cheese and wine
hotels.whyGo: The compact-room format on the Shoreditch edge of the City, with free cheese and wine in the lounge each evening.
hotels.opNote: SAME WINDOWLESS 'INSIDE' ROOMS as the Covent Garden branch - the cheapest rate has no window and people book it by accident. Pay up a grade unless you genuinely do not mind.

hotels.name: Aethos London Shoreditch
hotels.style: Members'-club-style boutique in a former Nobu Hotel
hotels.whyGo: A wellness-minded rebrand of the former Nobu Hotel Shoreditch - floor-to-ceiling windows, a members'-club feel, and an underground spa with steam and sauna, minutes from Brick Lane and Old Street.
hotels.opNote: Rooms lean small for the price band, which is the Shoreditch trade-off; the top-floor Skyline rooms with private balconies are the ones worth booking ahead for.

hotels.name: Batty Langley's
hotels.whyGo: Dark walls, floor-to-ceiling silk curtains, antiques and oil paintings on a cobbled Spitalfields street - closer to staying inside a Georgian house museum than a hotel.
hotels.opNote: Seven minutes from Liverpool Street. A period townhouse with no lift and no air conditioning; that is the trade for the atmosphere. Next door to Dennis Severs' House, which is the same idea as a museum.

hotels.name: Bermondsey Square Hotel
hotels.style: Independent, on the antiques market square
hotels.whyGo: Ninety rooms on the square that hosts Bermondsey's Friday antiques market, walking distance to Bermondsey Street, Maltby Street and the Beer Mile.
hotels.opNote: The rooftop rooms have private terraces and are worth the upgrade if available. Ask for a room away from the square on market mornings if noise matters.

hotels.name: Bingham Riverhouse
hotels.whyGo: A restored Grade II Georgian townhouse directly on the Thames, with a well-regarded restaurant and a private members club sharing the building.
hotels.opNote: A Georgian building with limited lift access - ask about stairs if that matters. The river-view rooms are worth the upgrade.

hotels.name: DoubleTree by Hilton London Greenwich
hotels.style: Modern hotel in the historic quarter
hotels.whyGo: A fifteen-minute walk from the Cutty Sark, the Old Royal Naval College and the National Maritime Museum, unlike the Peninsula hotels which are a DLR ride from all three.
hotels.opNote: In the historic World Heritage part of Greenwich rather than on the Peninsula - the better choice for anyone whose trip is about the Observatory and the market, not the O2.

hotels.name: Hilton London Angel Islington
hotels.style: Sleek chain hotel in fashionable Islington
hotels.whyGo: On Upper Street itself, five minutes from Angel station, in an area with more restaurants and bars per yard than almost anywhere else in London.
hotels.opNote: The best-placed dependable chain hotel for Upper Street. Rooms on the upper floors have City skyline views worth requesting.

hotels.name: Hilton London Paddington
hotels.whyGo: The original Great Western Royal Hotel of 1854, built into the station itself - you can walk from the platform to the lobby without going outside.
hotels.opNote: Attached directly to the station, which is the whole point for a Heathrow Express connection. Grand public rooms; guest rooms are more conventional.

hotels.name: Hyatt Regency London Stratford
hotels.whyGo: Built into the Westfield Stratford City complex itself, with Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park and the ArcelorMittal Orbit a short walk away.
hotels.opNote: The shopping centre is genuinely attached - useful in bad weather, less useful if the point of the trip is not shopping.

hotels.name: Locke at Broken Wharf
hotels.style: Studios with kitchens on the river
hotels.whyGo: Full kitchens and a washing machine, directly opposite Tate Modern across the Millennium Bridge - the format that makes a week in London affordable with children.
hotels.opNote: Priced per apartment rather than per person, so the value improves sharply with a family. Weekly rates are materially cheaper than seven nights.

hotels.name: London Marriott Hotel Canary Wharf
hotels.style: Business hotel on West India Quay
hotels.whyGo: Floor-to-ceiling windows over West India Quay and the towers of Canary Wharf, with nineteen event spaces that make it the estate's default conference hotel.
hotels.opNote: Genuinely business-oriented - the fitness centre and business centre are 24-hour. Quiet at weekends when the district itself empties out.

hotels.name: Mondrian Shoreditch
hotels.style: Design hotel with a year-round rooftop pool
hotels.whyGo: A heated rooftop pool and terrace open all year over Shoreditch, which is the reason guests pick this over the area's other design hotels.
hotels.opNote: The rooftop pool and bar draw a non-resident crowd at weekends - book a pool slot rather than assuming it will be quiet.

hotels.name: Novotel London Canary Wharf
hotels.whyGo: Bokan, the rooftop restaurant and bar, has one of the better elevated views in east London and is open to non-residents.
hotels.opNote: Priced below the Marriott for similar business-hotel amenities. The rooftop bar is worth visiting even if not staying.

hotels.name: One Hundred Shoreditch
hotels.whyGo: Whitewashed walls, tapestry hangings and pine, with cult DS & Durga toiletries - Time Out described it as staying in the spare room of an impossibly fashionable friend.
hotels.opNote: Formerly the Ace Hotel building. Six bars and restaurants including a rooftop, all open to non-residents.

hotels.name: Redchurch Townhouse
hotels.whyGo: Thirty-seven rooms in a 1970s interior with Cowshed products and a ground-floor Cecconi's - Soho House quality without needing to be a member.
hotels.opNote: No membership required, unlike Shoreditch House round the corner. Small and quiet for the area.

hotels.name: San Domenico House
hotels.whyGo: A small, Italian-furnished townhouse just off Sloane Square, run more like a private house than a hotel - a rooftop terrace with views over Chelsea.
hotels.opNote: Small - seventeen rooms - so it books out well ahead. Breakfast is served in the room or on the roof terrace rather than a dining room.

hotels.name: Sanderson London
hotels.whyGo: A Philippe Starck interior of soft curtains and surrealist touches around an eighty-foot Long Bar, on Berners Street a few minutes from Charlotte Street.
hotels.opNote: The Long Bar draws a non-resident crowd in the evening, which is part of the appeal or a reason to book elsewhere depending on preference.

hotels.name: St Ermin's Hotel, Autograph Collection
hotels.whyGo: Reached down a tree-lined courtyard off a busy Westminster street, with an elaborate plasterwork ceiling in the lobby and a genuine wartime intelligence history - MI6 met here.
hotels.opNote: Between St James's Park and Victoria stations, both walkable. The courtyard entrance means it is quieter than the address suggests.

hotels.name: The Ampersand Hotel
hotels.whyGo: A design-led boutique on a quiet residential street between the three free museums, decorated in themed floors - astronomy, geology, music, botany.
hotels.opNote: Two minutes from the South Kensington museum tunnel entrance, which most guests do not realise runs directly to the Natural History Museum.

hotels.name: The Chelsea Townhouse
hotels.whyGo: A Victorian townhouse of 35 individually decorated rooms with Edwardian antiques, on a residential garden square two minutes off the King's Road.
hotels.opNote: RENAMED FROM THE DRAYCOTT in 2022 - older reviews and articles still use the old name; do not treat them as a different hotel.

hotels.name: The Exhibitionist Hotel
hotels.style: Maximalist art hotel off Cromwell Road
hotels.whyGo: Every wall carries art - eight gallery-style spaces of rotating and permanent pieces, a deliberately maximalist answer to the neutral boutique hotel, a few minutes from the V&A and South Kensington station.
hotels.opNote: Rooms are on the small side for the rate, and reviewers are split on 100 Kensington, the in-house restaurant - book the room for the design, not the kitchen.

hotels.name: The Hoxton, Holborn
hotels.whyGo: The same lived-in lobby format as the Shoreditch original, minutes from the British Museum rather than the bar strip - the calmer of the two.
hotels.opNote: Breakfast bag included, same as the other Hoxtons. Recently refreshed rooms across the estate - ask whether a specific room has had the update if it matters.

hotels.name: The Hoxton, Shoreditch
hotels.whyGo: The hotel that made the open-lobby-as-workspace format normal, and still the best example of it - the ground floor is genuinely full of locals, not just guests.
hotels.opNote: Breakfast is a bag hung on your door, included in the rate. Room grades are named by SIZE - a Shoebox is exactly what it says.

hotels.name: The Hoxton, Southwark
hotels.whyGo: The Hoxton format applied to a Southwark new-build, with Seabird - a rooftop restaurant with the longest oyster list in London - on top.
hotels.opNote: Breakfast bag included in the rate, as at every Hoxton. Seabird on the roof is open to non-residents and needs booking.

hotels.name: The Laslett
hotels.style: Named for local artists and writers
hotels.whyGo: Every room named after a local artist, writer or musician associated with Notting Hill, on the doorstep of Portobello Road.
hotels.opNote: Right on Notting Hill Gate, so it is the most convenient of the area's boutiques for the Central and Circle lines.

hotels.name: The Megaro
hotels.whyGo: A 40-room independent recognisable from the street by the giant graffiti-style mural covering its whole facade, individually designed rooms and about as close to St Pancras as a hotel gets outside the Renaissance itself.
hotels.opNote: Genuinely independent and personally run, which shows in the service compared with the chains nearby. Small enough to book out for a Eurostar-timed stay.

hotels.name: The Pelican
hotels.whyGo: Rooms above one of the better gastropubs in west London, on All Saints Road a few minutes off Portobello.
hotels.opNote: A small pub with rooms rather than a hotel - no lift, no reception desk in the hotel sense. The dining room is the draw and books ahead.

hotels.name: The Petersham Hotel
hotels.style: Victorian hotel above the river meadows
hotels.whyGo: Perched above Petersham Meadows with the same protected river view Turner painted, a short walk from the top of Richmond Hill.
hotels.opNote: Book a river-view room specifically - standard rooms do not face the Thames. Steep walk down to the towpath and back up.

hotels.name: The Portobello Hotel
hotels.roomTypes: Double, suite, some with round beds and freestanding baths
hotels.whyGo: A 21-room Victorian townhouse on a quiet garden square, favoured by musicians and actors since the 1970s for exactly the reason it still works - nobody bothers you.
hotels.opNote: A townhouse with no lift, so upper rooms mean stairs with luggage. Some of the more theatrical rooms - round beds, claw-foot baths in the room itself - are not for everyone; ask before booking.

hotels.name: The Rubens at the Palace
hotels.whyGo: Directly opposite the Royal Mews, a two-minute walk from Buckingham Palace and under two blocks from Victoria station.
hotels.opNote: The closest genuinely comfortable hotel to Buckingham Palace and the Royal Mews on foot. Traditional, family-run styling rather than a design hotel.

hotels.name: The Standard, London
hotels.whyGo: A preserved 1974 Brutalist town hall annexe directly opposite St Pancras, with Shawn Hausman interiors described as Stanley Kubrick through the colour lens of Wes Anderson.
hotels.opNote: Decimo, the tenth-floor tapas restaurant, has the view. The external red lift running up the outside of the building is worth requesting a room near.

hotels.name: The Zetter Townhouse Marylebone
hotels.whyGo: A Georgian townhouse decorated like an eccentric relative's home - taxidermy, clashing prints, and a cocktail lounge that is a destination in its own right.
hotels.opNote: Small and stair-heavy in places despite the lift. The ground-floor bar gets busy with non-residents, which is either the charm or the problem.

hotels.name: Town Hall Hotel
hotels.whyGo: A 1910 town hall with the council chamber and marble staircases intact, a 14-metre heated pool, and the two-Michelin-starred Da Terra in the building.
hotels.opNote: TIME OUT'S BEST HOTEL IN LONDON. In Bethnal Green rather than the centre, which is the trade and the reason it costs half what a comparable central room would.

hotels.name: Treehouse Hotel London
hotels.whyGo: Occupies the top floors next to BBC Broadcasting House, so every room has a panorama - and the rooms come with magic 8 balls, cuckoo clocks and Paddington Bears without tipping into gimmick.
hotels.opNote: Time Out gave it FIVE out of five, calling it everything you could want from a sustainable yet high-end hotel in London's busiest district. The rooftop bar is open to non-residents.

hotels.name: Wilde Aparthotels Covent Garden
hotels.whyGo: A kitchen and a washing machine in the middle of the West End, which removes the single biggest cost of a London family trip - eating out three times a day.
hotels.opNote: Studios rather than separate bedrooms, so a family shares one room. Check the floor plan before booking for four. NOTE: the only named press review found for this brand covers Wilde's Paddington site, not this one - the two are different buildings and should not be assumed identical.

hotels.name: art'otel London Battersea Power Station
hotels.style: Design hotel with a rooftop pool
hotels.whyGo: Jaime Hayon's bold, colourful design throughout, a rooftop pool over the Power Station chimneys, and named Hotel of the Year 2025 by The Caterer.
hotels.opNote: Inside the Battersea Power Station development itself, so the shops, bars and Lift 109 are all a lift ride away rather than a walk.

hotels.name: Broadwick Soho
hotels.whyGo: Leopard print, velvet and clashing colour by Martin Brudnizki, built by a group of friends rather than a hotel group - and named the UK's best hotel at the 2026 Muddy Stilettos Awards, beating out the country's grandest countryside piles.
hotels.opNote: NATIONAL AWARD, not a London-only one - it beat entries from Bath, Hampshire, Wiltshire and Kent to take the UK title. Fifty-seven rooms, so it is small and books out.

hotels.name: Brown's Hotel
hotels.whyGo: Opened 1837 and generally called London's first hotel - Kipling wrote here, Bell made the first British telephone call from it, and Agatha Christie set At Bertram's Hotel on it.
hotels.opNote: A Michelin Key. The Drawing Room afternoon tea is open to non-residents and is the traditional way in.

hotels.name: Charlotte Street Hotel
hotels.style: Firmdale boho-chic on the restaurant street
hotels.whyGo: Fifty-two boho-chic rooms with a private screening room and a walk-in position on Charlotte Street itself, the densest restaurant run in central London.
hotels.opNote: The screening room can be booked privately, which is an unusual amenity to have on the doorstep of a dinner reservation rather than across town.

hotels.name: Claridge's
hotels.whyGo: The art deco hotel other London hotels are measured against, and the only London property on Conde Nast Traveller's 2026 Gold List.
hotels.opNote: Afternoon tea books months ahead and is the affordable way to see the building without a room. Dress code is enforced in the public rooms.

hotels.name: Corinthia London
hotels.style: Whitehall grand, with a four-floor spa
hotels.whyGo: Two Michelin Keys, a Baccarat chandelier of a thousand crystals in the lobby, and a spa running across four floors - the largest of any London hotel.
hotels.opNote: Between Trafalgar Square and the river, so Westminster and the South Bank are both walkable. Seven penthouse suites sit at the top.

hotels.name: Ham Yard Hotel
hotels.style: Firmdale's Soho flagship round a garden
hotels.whyGo: Two Michelin Keys, built from the ground up around a tree-filled courtyard with a Tony Cragg bronze, and a 1950s bowling alley in the basement.
hotels.opNote: Kit Kemp's patterns throughout, as at Charlotte Street. The bowling alley and the roof terrace are bookable without a room.

hotels.name: Hotel Café Royal
hotels.whyGo: Two Michelin Keys, a grand nineteenth-century building on the Soho edge of Regent Street, and the Akasha spa that Time Out named London's best in 2025.
hotels.opNote: The Grill Room and the Oscar Wilde Lounge are open to non-residents and are the affordable way to see the interiors.

hotels.name: InterContinental London - The O2
hotels.whyGo: A glass tower on the river with a spa and pool looking straight across to Canary Wharf, attached to The O2 for anyone catching a show there.
hotels.opNote: On the Peninsula rather than in Greenwich town - a DLR or riverboat ride from the Cutty Sark and the Observatory, not a walk.

hotels.name: Mandarin Oriental Mayfair
hotels.whyGo: Only fifty rooms, which makes it the most intimate of the recent Mayfair openings, on Hanover Square a minute from Oxford Circus.
hotels.opNote: Small by design and sold out far ahead. The group's original Hyde Park property is a different hotel entirely - check which one you are booking.

hotels.name: Raffles London at The OWO
hotels.whyGo: The Old War Office on Whitehall, where Churchill planned D-Day and Ian Fleming worked in naval intelligence, converted into 120 rooms with butler service.
hotels.opNote: Nine restaurants and bars on site, several open to non-residents - the cheapest way into the building without a room. Directly on Whitehall, so Downing Street and the Churchill War Rooms are a walk.

hotels.name: Rosewood London
hotels.whyGo: Two Michelin Keys, entered through a carriageway into a Belle Époque courtyard that cuts the noise of High Holborn out completely.
hotels.opNote: Between Covent Garden and Bloomsbury, walkable to both. Scarfes Bar has live jazz nightly and is open to non-residents.

hotels.name: Shangri-La The Shard, London
hotels.style: The highest hotel in western Europe
hotels.whyGo: Floors 34 to 52 of the Shard, with the infinity pool on the 52nd floor giving a view over London that no other hotel in the city can offer at any price.
hotels.opNote: One of the highest-scoring hotels found in this pass - 9.1 across nearly 3,000 reviews. The view is genuinely the product; a lower floor room here defeats the point.

hotels.name: Six Senses London
hotels.style: Wellness hotel in the old Whiteleys
hotels.whyGo: Six Senses' first UK property, inside the Grade II Whiteleys department store, with a spa running a magnesium pool and cryotherapy.
hotels.opNote: Opened after a three-year delay. The spa is the reason to choose it over the Mayfair five-stars, and it is bookable by non-residents.

hotels.name: St Pancras Renaissance Hotel London
hotels.whyGo: George Gilbert Scott's 1873 Gothic Revival masterpiece, restored after decades of dereliction, attached directly to the Eurostar terminal at St Pancras.
hotels.opNote: The building the Spice Girls filmed 'Wannabe' on the staircase of - a fact almost every guide mentions and almost every guest asks about. Book the Chambers Suites for the original 1873 rooms.

hotels.name: The Beaumont Mayfair
hotels.style: Art deco, with a sculpture you sleep inside
hotels.roomTypes: Double, suite, ROOM by Antony Gormley
hotels.whyGo: Two Michelin Keys, an art deco building on Brown Hart Gardens - and ROOM, an Antony Gormley sculpture bolted to the facade that you can book and sleep inside.
hotels.opNote: ROOM is a genuine Gormley artwork containing a bedroom, priced far above the standard rooms and booked months out. The rest of the hotel is a straightforwardly excellent deco five-star.

hotels.name: The Cadogan, A Belmond Hotel
hotels.whyGo: A Sloane Street address with a genuine history of hosting dignitaries and celebrities, restored by Belmond and consistently one of the best-reviewed hotels in the city.
hotels.opNote: One of the highest guest-rating scores of any hotel in London - 97% in the surveys collected. On Sloane Street itself, so the King's Road shops are a short walk.

hotels.name: The Connaught
hotels.style: Mayfair institution with a great bar
hotels.whyGo: The Connaught Bar has repeatedly been ranked the best bar in the world, and the Aman Spa in the basement is the quietest room in Mayfair.
hotels.opNote: The bar is open to non-residents and is the reason most people come. Book it - walk-ins at peak are turned away.

hotels.name: The Dorchester
hotels.style: Park Lane, with three Michelin stars in it
hotels.whyGo: Alain Ducasse at The Dorchester is one of the very few three-Michelin-star restaurants in the country, and it is in the building.
hotels.opNote: Five restaurants on site. The Promenade afternoon tea is the accessible one; Ducasse needs booking months ahead and is a separate proposition entirely.

hotels.name: The Emory
hotels.whyGo: Suite-only, from the Maybourne group behind Claridge's and The Connaught, with each floor given to a different designer - Andre Fu, Patricia Urquiola - and Jean-Georges overseeing the restaurant.
hotels.opNote: There are no standard rooms at all; the entry price is a suite. A rooftop Surrenne members' club sits on top.

hotels.name: The Goring
hotels.style: The last family-owned five-star in London
hotels.whyGo: Still owned by the Goring family after four generations, with a private garden behind and Buckingham Palace round the corner - the Princess of Wales stayed here the night before her wedding.
hotels.opNote: The only London five-star still in the hands of the family that built it. The garden is residents-only; the dining room is not.

hotels.name: The Langham, London
hotels.whyGo: Opened 1865 as Europe's first grand hotel, opposite BBC Broadcasting House, and the place afternoon tea in Britain was arguably formalised.
hotels.opNote: The Palm Court claims to be the birthplace of afternoon tea and books out well ahead. Conan Doyle and Oscar Wilde both dined here.

hotels.name: The Londoner
hotels.whyGo: Sixteen storeys, six of them below ground, including a private cinema and a subterranean ballroom - built into Leicester Square without dominating it.
hotels.opNote: Michelin calls it a super-boutique: boutique service at large-hotel scale. The rooftop bar looks over the square.

hotels.name: The Milestone Hotel
hotels.whyGo: A Victorian Gothic townhouse directly facing Kensington Palace and the Royal Gardens, with suites converted from the original carriage mews.
hotels.opNote: Each suite is individually themed and priced differently - the Stables suite, built from the original mews, is the one worth asking for by name.

hotels.name: The Ned
hotels.style: A 1924 bank turned hotel and members' club
hotels.whyGo: The former Midland Bank headquarters, built in 1924 by the architect the hotel is named for - marble banking hall, twelve restaurants, and a rooftop pool with St Paul's over the parapet.
hotels.opNote: The rooftop pool is for MEMBERS AND CERTAIN GUESTS ONLY - do not promise it to every booking. The basement spa's 20-metre pool is the one hotel guests can generally use.

hotels.name: The Peninsula London
hotels.whyGo: A purpose-built Peter Marino design at Hyde Park Corner, overlooking Wellington Arch and the gardens of Buckingham Palace.
hotels.opNote: Filed to the Westminster guide because that guide covers Victoria and St James's; Belgravia has no guide of its own and this sits on its Hyde Park Corner edge.

hotels.name: The Savoy
hotels.whyGo: The first luxury hotel in Britain to have electric light and en-suite bathrooms, on the only street in the country where traffic drives on the right.
hotels.opNote: River-view rooms cost substantially more and are the reason to stay. The American Bar is open to non-residents and is the cheaper way in.

hotels.name: The Soho Hotel
hotels.whyGo: Tucked down a mews off Dean Street behind a plain red-brick front, with two private screening rooms and a Botero cat in the lobby.
hotels.opNote: The Sunday film club - a screening plus lunch - is open to non-residents and is the best-value way in.
